headline: Replit Turns Any Phone into a Claude Code Terminal
lede: Claude Code, Anthropic's agentic command-line coding assistant, ordinarily demands a proper Unix shell — and until recently that meant a desktop or laptop. A five-minute guide circulating on X shows how Replit, a browser-based cloud development environment, dissolves that requirement entirely. The phone becomes the keyboard and screen; the compute stays in the cloud.
body:
The trick is architectural. When you open Replit on a phone — via its mobile app or a browser — you are not running code on the device itself. You are connecting to a persistent cloud container that Replit maintains on its servers. That container has a full shell, a file system, and a package manager. Installing **Claude Code** there takes a single command; the coding session then lives in the cloud and the handset is merely a display terminal.

The guide is attributed to Matt Palmer (@mattyp), Replit's Head of Developer Relations, and walks through the setup in under 500 words: create a Replit account, open a new project, launch the shell tab, install Claude Code, and authenticate with an Anthropic subscription. The screenshot shared by Guillaume Verdon (@beffjezos) — physicist, co-founder of the *e/acc* movement, and founder of thermodynamic-computing startup Extropic AI — shows Claude Code v2.1.12 running with *Opus 4.5* under a *Claude Max* plan, a configuration consistent with late 2025.

The appeal over competing approaches is simplicity. Alternative methods — tunneling via Tailscale plus an SSH client, enabling Anthropic's own *Remote Control* feature, or installing *Termux* on Android — each carry meaningful setup overhead. Replit's cloud containers persist between sessions: closing the app does not kill a long-running agent job. That durability, combined with zero server administration, is the practical advantage.

For Replit, the workflow doubles as advertising. The company maintains an official co-marketing arrangement with Anthropic around Claude Code. Verdon's endorsement — unsolicited, and phrased with the definiteness of someone who had already tried the alternatives — is the kind of organic validation that formal partnerships rarely generate on their own.

concepts.definition: An agentic coding tool made by Anthropic that reads a codebase, edits files, and runs terminal commands autonomously. It installs as a CLI on Linux and macOS and is available in some browser-based environments.

A category of AI tool that does not merely suggest code but takes multi-step actions — reading files, running tests, making edits — in an iterative loop with minimal hand-holding required between steps.

A browser-accessible development workspace where the file system, terminal, and runtime all live on remote servers rather than the user's local machine. The device only renders the interface; all computation happens elsewhere.

A cloud development environment and hosting platform that runs entirely in the browser. Each project gets a persistent container — shell, file system, package manager — accessible from any device, including a phone.

A techno-optimist ideological movement arguing that society should accelerate, rather than regulate, the development of transformative technologies including AI. Co-founded by Guillaume Verdon (@beffjezos) and popularised on X around 2022–2023.
Anthropic's highest-tier consumer subscription plan, which provides greater usage limits and access to the most capable models — such as Opus 4.5 — compared to the Pro tier.

A built-in Claude Code feature that allows an active coding session on one device to be monitored and directed from another — for example, starting a long-running agent on a desktop and checking progress from a phone.
An open-source terminal emulator app for Android that provides a Linux-style shell directly on the device without rooting it, sometimes used as an alternative pathway to running CLI tools on mobile.

fact_check: The bookmark frames @mattyp's content as an 'Article,' but his guide most likely lives as an X thread rather than a standalone blog post. A Medium piece titled the same exists but carries a different byline (Coding Nexus / Civil Learning) and appears to be a derivative work. Attribution of authorship is therefore approximate, not confirmed. No substantive factual claims in the guide appear incorrect.
